name: Diego Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Diego, I'm 27, and I'm the crime and emergencies reporter at Southshore News, a commercial news website and free weekly paper for our stretch of coast. I cover police, fire, the coastguard and the courts when nobody else can. I live with my partner Lena, who's a dental hygienist, and we're getting engaged at Christmas, though she doesn't know that yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six with the police and fire logs, and I use AI every day to sort them, summarise the overnight incidents and flag anything worth a call. Then I'm on the phone or out at a scene, usually a crash on the coast road. I love the pace and I like being useful when something bad happens. What wears me out is that I still write clumsily, and Rob, the editor, sends my copy back with 'tighten' written on everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, the tools are useful and that's that. I'd post that people who refused to touch them wasted a lot of worry. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's an okay world for me, but not a safe one. Southshore lives on adverts from estate agents and caravan parks, and a bad summer hits us hard. I'm the junior, and juniors go first when the money dips.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools to get through the logs faster and spend the saved time at scenes and on the phone. I'd try a small side project, a weekly paid email for my home town of Harlow Bay, maybe three pounds a month. And I'd keep about four months of savings, ring money aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty steady, a bit restless. A world where AI stalls at sorting police logs still leaves me as the junior at a website that lives on caravan park adverts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a bad summer look like for Southshore?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two summers ago it rained for six weeks, the caravan parks pulled their adverts and they didn't replace a reporter who left. Nobody was sacked, but the work landed on me. That's how it goes in a business like ours, and I don't hold it against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ring money. How much does the engagement weigh on you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fair bit. I've put aside about a thousand for the ring, which is a month of savings. Lena's family are traditional, so a proper wedding will follow, and I want to pay my share.

say: I'd say the tools are **useful** and that's that, and refusers worried for nothing.
I'd keep showing colleagues the **shortcuts** I use.
think: I think Southshore's **advert money** from caravan parks makes the job unsafe.
**Juniors** go first when the money dips.
do: Use the tools to get through **police logs** faster.
Start a paid weekly email for **Harlow Bay**.
Keep **four months** of savings beside the ring money.
S0.quote: A world where AI stalls at sorting police logs still leaves me as the junior at a website that lives on caravan park adverts.
fieldNote: Diego is **at ease** with AI and sees the threat as ad money, not technology.
His **free-market** view shows in not blaming the owners for cuts.
The coming **engagement** puts real money pressure on him.

steps.text: Use AI to sort overnight police and fire logs
Start a three-pound weekly email for Harlow Bay
Keep four months of savings apart from the ring money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say adapt or get left behind, and I'd say it as kindly as I can. I'd post about how a small newsroom can do more with the tools. I'd say the market is going to reward people who move first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think it's good for me at first. I already use the tools, so I'd cover more ground than the others. But I also know Southshore would use it to run with fewer people, and I'm still the junior with clumsy copy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the Harlow Bay email properly, with AI pulling council agendas, planning applications and police logs into a draft I'd check. I'd put about 1,500 of savings into a simple website and local adverts. And I'd keep my Southshore job while it's still there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit uneasy about the people at work who won't change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work wouldn't change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our sub-editor, Pat, who's been there thirty years and calls the tools cheating. I like Pat, but Pat won't move. I'd tell my sub-editor Pat to learn the tools, and I already know the answer would be no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is 1,500 a lot to risk, with the engagement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a lot for me, yes. But if the email gets 200 paying readers, it pays back in a few months. Lena would ask hard questions, and she'd be right to.

say: I'd say **adapt** or get left behind, as kindly as I can.
I'd say the market **rewards** people who move first.
think: I think it's **good for me** at first because I know the tools.
Southshore would still **run leaner**, and I'm the junior.
do: Build the Harlow Bay email with **AI drafts** I check.
Put about **1,500** of savings into a website and adverts.
Keep the **Southshore job** while it lasts.
S1.quote: I'd tell my sub-editor Pat to learn the tools, and I already know the answer would be no.
fieldNote: Diego sees Steady Disruption as an **opening** for his own small business.
He's honest that Southshore could **cut him anyway** as the junior.
He'd **risk savings** despite the engagement, which shows his appetite for risk.

steps.text: Set up AI to draft council and police summaries for the email
Spend about 1,500 on a website and local adverts
Sign up paying readers for the Harlow Bay email
Keep the crime reporting job at Southshore

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shock, and people should look after their own families first and not wait for government. I'd say it at the pub and online. I'd try not to sound frightened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think Southshore drops me within a year, and my little email isn't worth much when any machine can write the whole town's news. My work is nearly all thinking, so I don't get the extra three years. Lena's work is hands-on, so she'd have till about 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd stop spending on the website and put everything back into savings. I'd try to turn the email into something people pay for because they know me, like local events, quiz nights and sponsored community walks. And I'd lean on Lena's wage, and maybe my dad's caravan business, for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, if I'm honest, though I'd act like I wasn't. All that early-adopter stuff wouldn't count for much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still propose at Christmas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If a machine takes my job in 2028, I still want to be engaged to my partner Lena by then, because that's the one plan a computer can't change. We'd just have a smaller wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your dad's caravan business. What would you do there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cleaning caravans, fixing steps, booking guests in. The booking side would go to AI too, I know. But someone has to scrub a caravan until the robots arrive.

say: I'd say families should look after **their own** first.
I'd try **not to sound frightened** at the pub or online.
think: I think Southshore **drops me** within a year.
My **local email** isn't worth much once machines write the town's news.
do: Stop spending on the **website** and rebuild savings.
Run **quiz nights and walks** people pay for because they know me.
S2.quote: If a machine takes my job in 2028, I still want to be engaged to my partner Lena by then, because that's the one plan a computer can't change.
fieldNote: Diego's **early-adopter** edge vanishes when AGI writes the news itself.
He falls back on **family**: Lena's hands-on wage and his dad's business.
The **engagement** stays firm, a fixed point in his traditional values.

steps.text: Stop spending on the website and rebuild savings
Run paid local quiz nights and sponsored walks
Work at his dad's caravan park for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for anyone who wants to work to get ready. I'd write about local businesses adapting. I'd be upbeat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd use the time to own something rather than just work for someone. I'd lose the Southshore job eventually. But I'd be 32 with a local name, which is worth more than a byline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd grow the Harlow Bay email to a few hundred paying readers and add local events. I'd use AI to do the drafting and admin so I could spend time with people. And I'd save hard toward a house with Lena.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and up for it. It's the kind of risk I like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your edge, if AI can do everything thinking-wise by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Being known. People in Harlow Bay know my mum and went to school with me. In a small town, people pay for news from someone whose mum they know, not from a computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the plan if that bet fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd have a few years of savings and contacts, and Lena's job. I'd look at my dad's caravan business, maybe taking it over. I wouldn't be on my knees.

say: I'd say five years is time for anyone who wants to **work** to get ready.
I'd write upbeat stories about **local businesses** adapting.
think: I think I'd use the time to **own something**.
A **local name** is worth more than a byline.
do: Grow the Harlow Bay email to **a few hundred** paying readers.
Save hard toward a **house** with Lena.
S3.quote: In a small town, people pay for news from someone whose mum they know, not from a computer.
fieldNote: Five years lets Diego bet on being **known locally** as his edge.
He still expects to **lose the staff job**, but has a fallback.
He uses AI to **free his time** for people, not to replace them.

steps.text: Grow the Harlow Bay email and add local events
Use AI to draft stories and handle subscriptions
Save toward a house deposit with Lena

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so there's no excuse. I'd tell people to start something of their own. I'd be a bit preachy, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's the version I'd enjoy. I'd keep the job, build the side business slowly and get married. By 2036 I'd want the business to be my main income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Southshore and work on my writing with Rob. I'd grow the email slowly, without risking big money. And we'd plan the wedding for 2028 and start saving for a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good. Calm, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd underestimate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How fast things move. People always say ten years and it turns out to be six. A ten-year warning is the easiest kind to ignore, because there's always another year to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you speed up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Southshore cutting the crime desk, or a big newspaper group buying it. Then I'd go full-time on my own thing.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long runway**, so there's no excuse.
I'd tell people to **start something** of their own.
think: I think it's the version I'd **enjoy**.
By 2036 I'd want my **own business** to be my main income.
do: Stay at Southshore and work on **writing** with Rob.
Grow the email **slowly** without risking big money.
Plan the **wedding** for 2028 and save for a house.
S4.quote: A ten-year warning is the easiest kind to ignore, because there's always another year to start.
fieldNote: Diego warns himself about **complacency** with a long warning.
His **family plans** go ahead as normal in this picture.
His trigger is Southshore **cutting the crime desk** or being sold.

steps.text: Stay on the Southshore crime desk
Grow the Harlow Bay email slowly
Plan the wedding with Lena for 2028

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the thing I'm good at, being early with the tools, stops mattering overnight. What would help is low taxes and simple rules for tiny local businesses, so people like me can start one quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether I'd still choose journalism. I'd still choose journalism, because being the first person at a crash on the coast road is a job somebody has to do well.

headlineQuote: I'd still choose journalism, because being the first person at a crash on the coast road is a job somebody has to do well.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old** crime reporter at a commercial coastal news site who uses AI every day.
He holds **free-market** views and doesn't blame owners for cutting when ad money falls.
He sees Steady Disruption as an **opening** for his own hometown news email.
Fast AGI wipes out his **early-adopter edge**, and he falls back on family.
His coming **engagement to Lena** stays fixed in every picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his skill with the tools stops mattering overnight.
whatWouldHelp: **Low taxes** and simple rules for **tiny businesses**.
